d each problem

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| 263 orders confirmed for 250 units | `reserve`, `addStock`, `commit` and `release` each read a SKU's counters, change them and write them back, with nothing stopping another call doing the same in between. Two checkouts could both see the last unit as free, and one call's write could erase another's. |
| `reserved` went negative | `release()` never refused a committed order, although its doc comment says it can't be released. `expire()` released every old order whatever its status, so the nightly run took held units back a second time from orders that were already committed. A commit and a release racing on one order could also both apply. |
| Retry after a timeout held units twice | The "does this order already exist?" check and the write of the order were separate steps, so a retry arriving mid-flight passed the check too. |
| Bundle item stayed held | `reserve` held items one at a time and threw on the out-of-stock item without undoing the earlier ones. No order record was written, so neither `release` nor `expire` could ever find that hold. |
| `sold` higher than orders shipped | Two commits of the same order could both count its units. `expire()` also turned committed orders into released ones while their units stayed counted as sold. |

## The fix
- **`src/lock.js` (new):** a lock keyed by name. A call waits only for other calls on the same keys. Waiters are served in arrival order, and idle keys are dropped, so memory doesn't grow with the number of SKUs.
- **`src/inventory.js`:**
  - Anything that reads and then changes an order holds that order's lock. Counter changes hold the locks of their SKUs.
  - The order lock is always taken before any SKU lock, and SKU locks in sorted order, so two bundles can't deadlock.
  - A bundle's SKUs are all read and checked before anything is written.
  - `release()` now rejects a committed order with `OrderStateError`.
  - `expire()` releases only stale orders that are still reserved, checks that under the order's lock, and returns only the orders it released on that call.
  - Method signatures, return values and error classes are unchanged. `src/store.js` is untouched, and the service still uses only `get`, `set` and `keys`.

## Tests
- **`tests/inc-5521.test.js`:** one group per symptom. Each test failed on the original code and passes now. There is also a test that a call on one SKU finishes while a call on another SKU is stuck, and a random-traffic test that rebuilds every counter from the order records.
- **`tests/lock.test.js`:** tests for the lock itself.
- **Checking the tests catch the bugs:** I ran the new tests against deliberately broken versions: one service-wide lock, unsorted lock order, locks per service instance, no order lock, `release` accepting committed orders, and `expire` ignoring status. In every case the test aimed at that bug failed. The random-traffic test also passed with 150 different random seeds.

## Assumptions
- **Locks work within one process only.** Services created on the same store object share locks, so 40 workers in one process don't oversell. Workers in separate processes can't be coordinated using only `get`, `set` and `keys`; that would need atomic updates from the store itself.
- **No `destroy`/`close` method:** the lock has no timers and drops idle keys, so there is nothing to clean up.
- **Not committed:** the changes are uncommitted on `main`. You didn't ask for a commit, and there is no remote to push to.

## Follow-ups (not built)
- **Repair existing data:** this stops new drift but doesn't correct the SKUs whose `reserved` is already negative. Those need a one-off rebuild from the order records.
- **Store failures:** if a store write fails partway through a bundle, earlier writes stay in place. Fixing that needs transactions or rollback in the store.
- **Multiple processes:** coordinating workers across processes needs an atomic operation in the store, such as compare-and-set or a script.
